rewrites.summary:
Rwanda demands real caution from trans visitors. Same-sex intimacy is not criminalised, and the government formally tolerates a small LGBT presence — but a 2025 Human Rights First Rwanda Association submission to the UN Human Rights Committee documents ongoing law-enforcement abuses against transgender persons, including arbitrary arrests and detentions (framed as “vagrancy” or “deviance” round-ups in Kigali's periodic street-cleaning operations).

For a visitor: no statutory exposure, but Kigali's sweep operations can net gender-nonconforming people, and recourse is nil. There is no legal gender recognition and no anti-discrimination protection, and the constitution recognises only civil monogamous marriage between a man and a woman — a partner-travel consideration for a trans visitor.
rewrites.tangentialFactors:
Executive and legislative flux colour the picture without being core street risk: a 2016 presidential statement said LGBT life “hasn't been our problem. And we don't intend to make it our problem,” and NGO Law No. 058/2024 (adopted June 2024) raises freedom-of-association concerns for civil-society groups.

Historical context situates the country with its neighbours: anthropologists report that same-sex relations among young men existed before colonial administration but were private and secret, and the modern record is shaped by post-1994 genocide memory. This history informs the assessment but does not dominate it.
rewrites.localsOnly:
The sweep-detention abuses documented in the 2025 HRF submission primarily affect residents, though the sweep mechanism can catch visitors.

Civil society operates within the regime's tight limits: LGBTIQ organisations cannot register openly, and a public Pride event was held in 2021 under those constraints.
rewrites.outOfScopeNotes: Sweep detentions are documented against trans persons specifically (2025 HRF submission). No source in this record covers visa or border document screening for trans visitors, and implementation practice of the 2024 NGO law is unverified. The 2016 presidential statement is dated and may not reflect current policy.

rewrites.summary:
DR Congo is dangerous for trans visitors. Same-sex conduct has never been criminalised — but the reality on the ground is severe insecurity: mob justice against perceived LGBT people is documented, police extortion is routine, parts of the country are an active conflict zone (M23), and LGBT organisations (Savie asbl in Bukavu) report systematic violations in their 2024 universal periodic review submission. There is no legal gender recognition and no protection infrastructure; Kinshasa's small scene is underground.

For a visitor: no statutory exposure, but outing risks mob violence with no effective protection anywhere in the country. Public same-sex affection can be prosecuted under indecent-exposure provisions (Article 176 of the Penal Code, rarely invoked), and same-sex marriage is constitutionally banned, so a trans visitor's partner has no recognition.
rewrites.tangentialFactors:
The security backdrop is broader than LGBT risk: a 2017 investigation documented security forces recruiting former M23 fighters and deploying them with orders to use lethal force against protesters, and armed groups (including M23) commit extreme violence against LGBTQ people with near-total impunity — context for why legal protections remain theoretical.

The 2024 universal periodic review submission is the active international mechanism tracking these abuses, with no government response yet weighed in the sources; this is adjacent process, not a core local risk.
rewrites.localsOnly:
Local LGBT organisations such as Savie asbl in Bukavu report systematic violations in their 2024 universal periodic review submission — a resident-specific reporting record of police and mob abuses; church groups promote the view that homosexuality is immoral.

For residents there is no legal gender change and no gender-identity recognition, and Kinshasa's small scene operates underground.
rewrites.outOfScopeNotes: Conflict conditions in the east are general; mob justice against LGBT people is documented in universal periodic review submissions. No source covers visa or border document handling for trans visitors. The Article 176 indecency provision is rarely invoked but its contemporary charging practice is verified only through the 2025 freshness confirmation that it is still occasionally used.

rewrites.summary:
Haiti is dangerous for trans visitors. Same-sex conduct is legal, but the national government has effectively collapsed: gangs control most of the capital (Port-au-Prince), the police are outgunned, and mob violence against perceived LGBT people is documented. There is no legal gender recognition, no protection infrastructure, and no functioning judiciary.

The trans-specific risk is inseparable from the generalised collapse — outing in gang-controlled areas can be lethal. A 2018 official US State Department report described attitudes as hostile toward LGBTI individuals who were public and visible about their sexual orientation or gender identity, particularly in the capital; freshness confirms trans people remain exposed to vagrancy-law fines with zero protection or hate-crime coverage.
rewrites.tangentialFactors:
Legislative flux: in 2017 the senate passed a bill banning same-sex marriage and public LGBT advocacy (up to three years' imprisonment and a large fine for parties), and a 2017 bill would have allowed denial of the good-conduct certificate demanded by employers and universities on grounds of homosexuality; both awaited a vote in the other chamber as of November 2017, and their current status is unverified in the sources.

A regional LGBT advocacy body issued a mourning statement after the 2019 activist death — an adjacent regional reaction rather than a local policy finding.
rewrites.localsOnly:
Residents face documented hostility: a 2018 official US State Department report described attitudes as remaining hostile toward LGBTI individuals who were public and visible about their sexual orientation or gender identity, particularly in the capital, and the 2018 world human-rights report recorded that LGBT persons continued to face high levels of discrimination.

The president of the national LGBTQ advocacy organisation was found dead at his home in 2019, with poisoning unconfirmed — a resident-protection data point rather than a documented pattern. The good-conduct certificate that employers and universities require could be denied on grounds of homosexuality under the 2017 senate bill, a mechanism affecting residents who need it for work or study.
rewrites.outOfScopeNotes: Collapse of national governance is general; mob violence against LGBT people is documented but not quantified. The status of the 2017 senate action at the other legislative chamber is unverified in the sources. No source covers visa or border document handling for trans visitors.

rewrites.summary:
Vanuatu demands real caution from trans visitors. Same-sex conduct is legal (never criminalised) with no legal gender recognition; there is a small VPride community in Port Vila, and kastom and church conservatism — but no documented anti-trans violence pattern.

Direct risk signals for visitors: in November 2024 the government moved to develop a national policy banning LGBTQIA+ advocacy and promotion, framed as contrary to constitutional and Christian values, and the Marriage Act was amended to define marriage as the union of a male and a female, so same-sex marriages cannot be registered — a partner-travel consideration.
rewrites.tangentialFactors: Institutional turbulence: in November 2024 a ministry was to appoint a committee to draft a national policy banning LGBTQIA+ advocacy and promotion, following a council-of-ministers decision earlier that year — an active policy process whose scope, timeline and enforcement are not yet documented.
rewrites.localsOnly:
The local VPride community (established 2014) faced church, official and chief opposition at founding; a joint 2016 human-rights workshop found same-sex partners get no protection under the Family Protection Act 2008 and must rely on penal-code routes, and a law lecturer documented only one prosecuted violence-against-lesbians case with a near-invisible LGBTI court presence.

Kastom and church conservatism shape resident attitudes, framing LGBTQIA+ expression as contrary to cultural values — with no documented anti-trans violence pattern among residents.
rewrites.outOfScopeNotes: Thin data: only three usable sources, no freshness re-check of the 2024 policy developments, and no source covers visa or border document handling for trans visitors. The drafted policy's scope, timeline and enforcement are unverified.

There is no criminalisation of same-sex conduct (some constituent parts historically had provisions), sexual-orientation discrimination has been illegal since a 2018 constitutional equality reform, there is no legal gender recognition, and no anti-trans pattern is documented.

For a visitor the protections are administrative rather than police-backed: no documented anti-trans violence or enforcement pattern exists, and the two archived reports (2010, 2015) are superseded by the 2018 reform.

rewrites.summary:
The Republic of the Congo is dangerous for trans visitors. Same-sex conduct is legal (never criminalised) — but the 2024 official assessment (EUAA COI) documented societal discrimination, police harassment (including bribes extracted under an ambiguous 'acts against nature' provision) and the absence of protection; there is no legal gender recognition, and only a small underground community.

For a visitor: no statutory exposure to a criminalisation regime, but the ambiguous under-21 'shameless act / acts against nature' provision has been used to justify discrimination and, in police practice, to extract bribes; no arrests or prosecutions under it were reported in 2022 or 2023.
rewrites.tangentialFactors: The discrepancy between a higher same-sex age of consent and its prosecution practice is an adjacent legal-flux point: the penal provision sets a higher age of consent (21) for same-sex conduct than for different-sex conduct (18), and its scope is 'ambiguous' — a basis for discrimination noted by both the 2024 official assessment and the 2022/2023 official reports.
rewrites.localsOnly: Resident-facing: NGOs reported violence, psychological and physical harassment, and financial extortion of LGBTQI+ persons by both government and nonstate actors in 2022 and continuing in 2023, with no anti-discrimination protections in law.
rewrites.outOfScopeNotes: The official assessment documents the harassment pattern; it is qualitative and does not quantify incidence. No source covers visa or border document handling for trans visitors, and no source documents legal gender recognition practice. The age-of-consent provision's application to trans persons specifically is unreported.

blindSourceSummaries: An official country-of-origin assessment (May 2024): systematic review of legislation, implementation, treatment by official institutions and society, and availability of official protection for LGBTQI+ people; no law criminalises consensual same-sex conduct, a penal article sets a higher age of consent for same-sex acts, and that provision's scope is described as 'ambiguous' and used to justify discrimination.

rewrites.summary:
The Central African Republic is dangerous for trans visitors. Same-sex conduct is legal, and public same-sex affection display is criminalised under public-morals provisions — the current overview per freshness — while national administration barely exists outside the capital: armed groups control most areas, mob violence and police extortion against perceived LGBT people are documented, legal gender recognition is not permitted, and there is no community infrastructure.

For a visitor: nothing protects, and same-sex marriage is constitutionally banned (defined as a union between one man and one woman); a trans visitor travelling with a partner has no recognition, and public affection can be prosecuted under the public-morals provisions.
rewrites.tangentialFactors:
The general security collapse — extrajudicial killings, torture and rape by security forces and armed factions documented since 2012 — is the dominant backdrop and affects everyone, not specifically LGBT people; it informs the assessment but does not define visitor risk beyond the absence of protection.

Policy framing is contested: SOGI issues are treated as taboo and as 'imported'/'contrary to local values' per a 2019 overview, and a 2024 stakeholder review process carried SOGI-related recommendations within a thin institutional framework — adjacent process rather than resolved policy.
rewrites.localsOnly: Resident-facing: legal gender recognition is not permitted and LGBTQI+ persons cannot serve openly in the military; no anti-discrimination provisions exist in law, and no known organisations promoting LGBTQI+ rights were documented in the 2023 official report — public-space criminalisation pushed the community underground.
rewrites.outOfScopeNotes: Thin data, with an absence-of-authority profile: the 2023 report copy contained no extractable text, and the 2023 official report is flagged as superseded by newer practice per freshness. No source covers visa or border document handling for trans visitors, and the exact charging practice under the public-morals provisions is unreported.

For a visitor: nothing protects, and same-sex marriage is constitutionally banned (defined as a union between one man and one woman); a trans visitor travelling with a partner has no recognition, and public affection can be prosecuted under the public-morals provisions.
